overview: Fletcher Building is New Zealand's largest building materials, distribution and residential development group, manufacturing and distributing products such as plasterboard, insulation, laminates, pipes, cement, concrete, aggregates and steel across New Zealand and Australia, alongside a plumbing/building products distribution network and a residential land/homes development business. FBU.AX is an ASX Foreign Exempt Listing (secondary quotation); the company's primary listing, statutory reporting entity and governance home is the NZX (ticker FBU.NZ), and it reports in NZ dollars. FY2026 marked a strategic turning point: after completing the sale of its Construction division to VINCI (effective 29 May 2026) and exiting Tradelink, Steel reinforcing/wire and other non-core assets, Fletcher is now a more focused building-products manufacturing and distribution group operating through Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution and Residential & Development.

business_model.summary: Fletcher earns margin as a vertically-integrated manufacturer and distributor of building materials (plasterboard, insulation, laminates/panels, piping, cement, aggregates, concrete, steel) sold to trade, merchant, commercial and residential construction customers in New Zealand and Australia, supplemented by a NZ building/plumbing products distribution network (PlaceMakers, Tradelink historically) and a New Zealand/Australia residential land and housing development business that monetises land banks through home and section sales. Revenue is largely transactional/project-based (tied to residential and commercial construction volumes) rather than recurring, though distribution and some manufacturing lines have repeat trade-customer relationships. FY26 continuing-operations revenue was $5,994m (+7.3% YoY) with EBIT before Significant Items of $414m (+26%); the Group returned to net profit of $228m in FY26 (including discontinued operations) after net losses of -$419m (FY25) and -$227m (FY24), driven by large one-off Significant Items (restructuring, legacy legal/product-liability provisions, impairments and divestment losses) rather than a swing in underlying trading.

revenue_streams.name: Light Building Products (plasterboard, laminates/panels, insulation, piping)
Heavy Building Materials (cement, aggregates, concrete, steel NZ/Australia)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/trade — builders, merchants, plumbers, developers and commercial/residential construction contractors in New Zealand and Australia; Residential & Development also sells directly to homebuyers/investors
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly New Zealand with a substantial Australian manufacturing and distribution footprint (particularly Light Building Products/Laminex, Iplex pipes, and Steel/Heavy Building Materials); reports in NZD with AUD translation exposure

main_competitors: Winstone/other independent NZ building product manufacturers
Bunnings/Mitre 10 (trade merchant channel competitors to Distribution)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest and most vertically integrated building materials group in New Zealand, with a leading position in plasterboard, cement, insulation, concrete and piping domestically, and a meaningful but more fragmented/competitive presence in Australian building products (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit, Steel) where it holds a lower relative share against larger global players

moat_factors.factor: Vertical integration and manufacturing scale in NZ
moat_factors.description: Ownership of cement (Golden Bay), aggregates (Winstone Aggregates), plasterboard (Winstone Wallboards) and concrete production gives cost and logistics advantages difficult for smaller NZ competitors to replicate given the country's small, geographically dispersed market

PlaceMakers and other NZ distribution branches provide trade-customer reach and bundled product/logistics convenience, though margins are thin (Distribution division ROIC just 1.4% in FY26) and the segment faces intense price competition

Long-established New Zealand brands (Winstone, Golden Bay, PlaceMakers, Firth, Laminex) carry trade and consumer recognition built over decades, but brand strength has been dented by the multi-year run of product-defect and legacy-liability headlines

Products specified into NZ Building Code compliance pathways and long-standing trade relationships create switching costs for builders/merchants, though this is a shared industry dynamic rather than unique to Fletcher

weaknesses: History of costly product-liability and construction-defect events (Iplex/Typlex Pro-Fit polybutylene pipes in Western Australia, historic leaky-building/weathertightness liabilities, asbestos-related claims, Laminex Australia silicosis claims) that recur as fresh Significant Items year after year and damage trust

Group ROIC remains structurally below cost of capital (5.3% before Significant Items in FY26, up from 4.1% in FY25 but still well under WACC), with Distribution (1.4% ROIC) and Steel businesses flagged by management as sub-hurdle
Thin, price-competitive Distribution margins and exposure to volatile, cyclical NZ/Australia residential and commercial construction volumes
Complex multi-divisional, multi-country structure historically made execution and accountability difficult, prompting the FY25-26 divisional restructuring and decentralisation push
ASX listing is a secondary (Foreign Exempt) quotation with lower liquidity than the NZX primary listing; ASX investors are exposed to AUD/NZD translation on a NZD-denominated, NZX-governed security

growth_drivers: Portfolio simplification into a focused building-products manufacturing and distribution group following the Construction divestment (VINCI, completed 29 May 2026) and planned Fletcher Reinforcing & Wire/CSP Pacific/Vivid Living exits (targeted 1Q FY27), intended to lift Group ROIC toward its cost of capital

Adoption of Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) as the central value metric and a decentralised operating model with business-unit accountability against industry-specific WACC hurdles, already showing 13 of 19 core business units improving ROIC year-on-year in FY26

Balance sheet repair: net debt down to $637m at 30 June 2026 (from $999m a year earlier), within the middle of the target range, USPP notes repaid, new bank facilities and extended syndicated debt maturities pushed to FY28, supporting eventual dividend resumption

Capacity investments in core manufacturing (Firth's new Auckland batching plant, Fletcher Insulation's Sonata Acoustics facility, Winstone Aggregates recycled-aggregate capacity, Laminex NZ's new Taupō plant) positioning for share gains and margin improvement as volumes recover
Anticipated cyclical recovery in New Zealand residential and civil construction demand from calendar year 2027, plus early signs of stabilisation in parts of the Australian portfolio

Ongoing strategic review of the Residential & Development division (reported market estimates ~$850m), which could crystallise value and further simplify the portfolio toward core manufacturing/distribution
Continued cost-out programme (~$45m of year-to-date SG&A/warehouse savings called out at 1H FY26) supporting margin expansion independent of a volume recovery

business.description: Revenue and volumes are directly tied to New Zealand and Australian residential, civil and commercial construction activity, which remained subdued through FY26 with management not expecting a meaningful recovery until calendar 2027

An active strategic review of the Residential & Development division (potential full or partial divestment) creates execution risk and management distraction, and any outcome (retain, partial sale, or full exit) changes the Group's earnings mix and risk profile
Ongoing price competition in NZ trade distribution kept Distribution ROIC at just 1.4% in FY26, one of two segments explicitly flagged by management as below acceptable returns
Steel businesses (being divested as Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire/CSP Pacific) also below cost-of-capital returns, reflected in the FY26 write-down/loss on planned sale ($22m Significant Item)

financial.risk: No dividend / cash generation still recovering
financial.description: No dividend declared for FY24, FY25 or FY26; the Board has stated dividends will only resume once the Group generates positive free cash flow and net debt is in the lower half of the target range, meaning equity holders currently receive no income return

Despite improvement, net debt of $637m plus $1.2bn+ of lease liabilities remains material against a Group returning only modestly to profitability; Moody's rating was withdrawn (at the company's request) in June 2026 at Baa3 stable, removing an independent credit signal for investors

Five consecutive years of large one-off charges (-$252m FY17, -$276m FY20, -$301m FY23, -$333m FY24 and -$644m/-$565m FY25 including discontinued operations) mean reported statutory earnings remain unreliable as a guide to underlying performance and further legacy items could still emerge

financial.risk: Substantial share dilution from recent equity raises
financial.description: Weighted average shares outstanding rose from ~783m to 1,013m (Nov-2024 $700m capital raise, ~$680m net proceeds) to 1,075m by FY26, permanently diluting per-share metrics versus the pre-crisis share count

regulatory.risk: Iplex/Typlex Pro-Fit polybutylene pipe defects (Western Australia)
regulatory.description: Iplex Pipelines Australia's Pro-Fit pipe (sold 2017-2022) has suffered plumbing failures in WA homes; a joint industry response with the WA Government (~A$155m/NZ$170m provision, ~$168m to be spent over five years, 15-year complaints window) was finalised in FY25, but the Group incurred a further $10m of legal costs in FY26 managing claims and disputes, and residual claims/disputes (including builder group BGC legal action) remain an open-ended cost and reputational risk

Legacy New Zealand leaky-building claims and asbestos-related provisions (including Laminex Australia silicosis claims, with a further $6m provision increase in FY26) continue to generate periodic Significant Items decades after the underlying products/exposures occurred, evidencing a long tail of product-liability risk embedded in the Group's history

SkyCity is suing Fletcher (via the now-divested Construction business, with liabilities retained by Fletcher Building) for NZ$330m in damages over New Zealand International Convention Centre completion delays (handed over ~6.5 years late, opened February 2026); Fletcher has stated it will vigorously defend the claim beyond liquidated damages already paid, but an adverse outcome would fall on the parent given retained legacy construction liabilities

Despite selling the Construction division to VINCI, Fletcher retained legacy vertical-project liabilities and recognised a further $60m of provisions plus $13m of legal/overhead costs in FY26 for claims and disputes on projects it no longer operates but remains contractually exposed to

macro.description: NZ residential and civil demand remained subdued through FY26 with management explicitly stating a more meaningful recovery is not anticipated until calendar year 2027, directly affecting Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution and Residential & Development volumes

Early signs of stabilisation are emerging in parts of the Australian portfolio but conditions remain uneven, and rising input costs plus macro/political uncertainty are reported to be delaying or cancelling new commercial projects into 1H FY27

A meaningful share of revenue and costs are in AUD (Laminex Australia, Iplex Australia, Stramit, Steel); NZD/AUD average rate moved from 0.9138 to 0.8651 year-on-year in FY26 (a 5.3% shift), affecting reported NZD results

As a leveraged, capital-intensive manufacturer serving cyclical construction end-markets, Fletcher's volumes and funding costs are sensitive to NZ/Australia interest-rate trajectories; funding costs fell to $64m in FY26 from $93m in FY25 partly on lower debt and partly on rate relief

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand and Australian residential and commercial construction activity has been in a multi-year downturn through FY24-FY26 amid high interest rates, weak consumer/business confidence and reduced new-build activity; management and most commentators expect a more meaningful volume recovery to emerge only from calendar year 2027 as rate cuts flow through to housing starts and civil/infrastructure pipelines normalise
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — Fletcher's core manufacturing, distribution and residential development businesses are directly geared to new-build volumes and renovation activity in New Zealand and Australia, making revenue and margins strongly cyclical around the construction cycle, amplified by operating leverage in capital-intensive manufacturing
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — construction and housing demand (and hence Fletcher's volumes) are acutely sensitive to mortgage and business borrowing rates in both New Zealand and Australia; the Group's own funding costs also move with rates given remaining net debt and lease liabilities
key_input_costs: Energy (cement/aggregates production, notably Golden Bay Cement)
Raw materials for plasterboard, insulation, laminates and PVC/plastics for piping
Labour and contractor costs across NZ/Australia manufacturing and distribution operations

recent_developments.event: Fletcher Building announced the sale of its Construction division to VINCI Construction (transaction valued at $315.6m, potentially up to $334.1m), a major milestone in the Group's portfolio simplification strategy, with proceeds earmarked for debt reduction

1H FY26 results: revenue from continuing operations of $2,866m (broadly flat on pcp), EBIT before Significant Items of $145m (5.1% margin), net cash from operating activities improved to $156m (from $87m pcp), net debt of $1,164m below internal expectations, ~$0.8bn available liquidity; no interim dividend declared; management flagged NZ residential/civil demand staying subdued through FY26 with recovery not expected until calendar 2027, and early signs of stabilisation in parts of the Australian portfolio

NZ International Convention Centre (NZICC) reached Practical Completion and was handed over to SkyCity ahead of its February 2026 opening, closing out one of the Group's highest-profile legacy construction liabilities operationally, though the associated SkyCity litigation over delays continues

SkyCity's NZ$330m damages lawsuit against Fletcher over NZICC construction delays proceeded through the New Zealand courts; Fletcher has stated it will vigorously defend the claim, noting it has already paid liquidated damages capped under the original contract

Completion of the Construction division sale to VINCI on 29 May 2026 (final consideration ~$334m subject to completion adjustments), generating a $120m net gain on disposal recognised as a Significant Item; Fletcher retained certain legacy vertical-project liabilities and provisions

Fletcher Building repaid its US Private Placement notes, arranged new bank facilities and extended syndicated debt terms (pushing the next material debt maturity to FY28), and asked Moody's to withdraw its credit rating (effective 25 June 2026, at Baa3 stable at the time)

FY2026 full-year results (year ended 30 June 2026): revenue $5,994m (+7.3%), EBIT before Significant Items $414m (+26%), including ~$52m of earnings from surplus property sales; net earnings (including discontinued operations) of $228m, a $647m swing from FY25's $419m loss — the Group's first positive net earnings from continuing operations since FY23; net debt reduced to $637m (from $999m); ROIC before Significant Items improved to 5.3% (4.7% ex property sales) from 4.1% in FY25; no FY26 dividend declared, with dividend policy to be reset once the Group generates positive free cash flow and net debt is in the lower half of the target range

Management disclosed that macro uncertainty, rising input costs and election-related caution were delaying or cancelling new commercial projects, expected to weigh on 1H FY27 performance, with Residential volumes likely to remain below the prior year; FY27 capital expenditure guided to decrease to approximately $170m

Strategic review of the Residential & Development division confirmed as underway, with the company stating it is talking to a number of interested parties and that all options — including possible full divestment — remain open; market estimates have put the division's value at roughly $850m; no final decision had been announced as of this review

FY2026 statutory Annual Report signed and dated 18 August 2026, formally confirming the divisional restructuring effective 1 July 2025 (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution, Residential & Development, with Construction/Steel/Vivid Living/CSP Pacific/Tradelink all now discontinued operations) and detailing $10m of further Iplex Australia WA pipe legal costs and $73m of retained legacy construction provisions/costs recognised in FY26

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report and results announcement (18 August 2026)

items.notes: Management lifted FY26 EBIT guidance during the year on stronger Q4 volumes (partly pull-forward buying ahead of price rises and favourable weather in civil/infrastructure) and ~$52m of surplus property sale gains; actual result of $414m came in above the raised guidance range
Guided down from FY26 levels, reflecting continued capital discipline as part of the Group's balance sheet and ROIC-focused strategy

items.target: Softer half; commercial project delays/cancellations expected, Residential volumes below prior year
items.notes: No specific quantitative guidance given for 1H FY27 due to macro, political and election-related volatility; management explicitly flagged rising input costs and uncertainty as delaying or cancelling new commercial projects

items.target: No dividend; policy to be reset once positive free cash flow achieved and net debt in lower half of $400-900m target range
items.notes: Consistent with FY24-FY26 guidance; net debt of $637m at 30 June 2026 sits in the middle, not yet the lower half, of the target range

items.target: Meaningful NZ residential/civil recovery not expected until calendar year 2027
items.notes: Reiterated consistently from 1H FY26 through FY26 full-year commentary; Australian conditions described as showing early stabilisation but remaining uneven

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Peter Crowley and MD/CEO Andrew Reding said the portfolio is now simpler, net debt is inside the target range, and the Group has returned to profit, but cautioned that 'Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) for the Group is still below acceptable levels' and that management is 'determined to continue to focus on improving returns.' They specifically flagged Distribution (1.4% ROIC) and the Steel businesses as still below acceptable levels relative to cost of capital, calling out 'lifting these returns further' as 'a key focus for FY27.' On the outlook, management said New Zealand residential and civil demand is 'likely to remain relatively subdued through FY26, with a more meaningful recovery not anticipated until calendar year 2027,' while 'early signs of stabilisation are emerging' in parts of the Australian portfolio, 'although conditions remain uneven.'

bull_case: Deep structural turnaround underway: portfolio simplified via the Construction divestment to VINCI and exit of Tradelink, Steel reinforcing/wire and other non-core assets, refocusing the Group on core building-products manufacturing and distribution where it holds genuine New Zealand scale advantages

Balance sheet materially de-risked — net debt down from $999m to $637m in one year, USPP notes repaid, credit facilities extended to FY28, and the Group posted its first positive continuing-operations net earnings since FY23 in FY26

New ROIC-based capital discipline and decentralised operating model are already showing traction (13 of 19 core business units improved ROIC year-on-year in FY26), with a credible path to eventually clearing cost-of-capital hurdles and resuming dividends

Optionality from the ongoing Residential & Development strategic review (market estimates ~$850m) could crystallise value or further streamline the Group toward higher-return manufacturing/distribution operations

Deeply depressed starting point (NZ/Australia construction near cycle trough, management guiding recovery from CY2027) means even a modest cyclical upturn in volumes could translate into outsized earnings growth given the Group's operating leverage
bear_case: Recurring, seemingly unending run of large one-off Significant Items (five of the last ten fiscal years featuring $250m+ charges, including a record -$644m in FY25) makes statutory results unreliable and signals the Group's risk-management and quality-control track record remains a live concern rather than a resolved legacy issue

Iplex/Typlex Pro-Fit pipe defects in Western Australia carry a 15-year complaints window and continue to generate fresh legal costs each year ($10m in FY26 alone), while the SkyCity NZICC lawsuit (NZ$330m claim) and other retained legacy construction liabilities remain unresolved despite the Construction division sale

Group ROIC of just 5.3% (4.7% excluding property sale gains) remains well below cost of capital, with Distribution (1.4%) and Steel businesses explicitly called out by management as sub-hurdle, indicating the turnaround is still early-stage rather than proven

No dividend since FY23 and no fixed resumption date, meaning equity holders bear full cyclical and legacy-liability risk with no income return in the interim, on a share count that has grown ~37% (783m to 1,075m) since the FY24-25 distress

Business remains highly cyclical and geared to a New Zealand/Australia construction downturn that management itself does not expect to meaningfully recover until calendar year 2027, with 1H FY27 explicitly flagged as softer on delayed/cancelled commercial projects and weak Residential volumes
